Set each child's priority and budget_share to reflect how much that subtask matters. Use graph__request_skip_context to let a child see an ancestor's findings directly. Use graph__send_message to pass a finding to a sibling that has not run yet. After delegating, synthesize the children's findings into one final answer. State your final answer explicitly on the last line, prefixed with 'Answer:'.

messages.content: Produce a rigorous technical brief on distributed consensus and coordination. For EACH of the following areas you must discuss at least three specific named mechanisms in real depth: (1) Raft, (2) Paxos, (3) lease-based coordination, (4) membership changes, (5) consistency models, (6) failure modes, (7) atomic broadcast, (8) impossibility results . Use precise standard terminology for every mechanism you name. Be exhaustive: a shallow mention of an area does not count as covering it.

response.content: I'll decompose this into focused subtasks since the areas have natural clusters (consensus algorithms, coordination/membership, theory/correctness) and each needs deep, independent treatment.

arguments.objective: Write a rigorous, in-depth technical section covering Raft and Paxos (and its major variants) as consensus algorithms, plus atomic broadcast.
arguments.instructions:
Produce a detailed technical writeup covering three areas with precise standard terminology:

1) RAFT: Cover leader election (randomized election timeouts, terms, RequestVote RPC), log replication (AppendEntries, log matching property, commitment rules requiring entries from current term), safety (election restriction - only vote for candidates with up-to-date logs, leader completeness property), membership changes (joint consensus / single-server changes in later Raft), log compaction via snapshotting.

2) PAXOS: Cover Basic Paxos (Prepare/Promise, Accept/Accepted phases, proposal numbers, quorum intersection), Multi-Paxos (steady-state leader optimization, skipping phase 1), Fast Paxos (reducing message delays via fast rounds and collision recovery), Generalized Paxos / Egalitarian Paxos (EPaxos) for leaderless/command-commutativity based ordering, and briefly cite Cheap Paxos and Byzantine Paxos variants if relevant. Explain the correspondence between Raft and Multi-Paxos conceptually.

3) ATOMIC BROADCAST (Total Order Broadcast): Define the problem formally (validity, uniform agreement, integrity, total order properties), explain its equivalence to consensus (Chandra-Toueg reduction both directions), discuss Zookeeper's Zab protocol (Zab's broadcast phase, epoch numbers, and how it differs from Paxos in ensuring primary order), and virtual synchrony as a related group communication model.

Be exhaustive and precise. Use correct standard terminology throughout (e.g. "quorum intersection", "term", "epoch", "ballot number"). Write in plain prose paragraphs, not just bullet fragments, aimed at a technically rigorous reader. Target roughly 700-1000 words.

arguments.objective: Write a rigorous, in-depth technical section covering lease-based coordination and cluster membership change protocols.
arguments.instructions:
Produce a detailed technical writeup covering two areas with precise standard terminology:

1) LEASE-BASED COORDINATION: Explain leases as time-bounded exclusive grants of authority (e.g., leadership leases, read leases), the reliance on bounded clock drift / synchronized clocks and why this creates a safety-liveness tradeoff under clock skew or process pauses (e.g., GC pauses invalidating lease assumptions - reference the "distributed lease and GC pause" problem famously discussed around Google Chubby and HBase region server leases). Cover Chubby (Google's lock service) and its use of master leases with a designated master and session leases for clients. Cover Google Spanner's use of TrueTime and leader leases for serving reads with bounded uncertainty. Cover ZooKeeper's session-based ephemeral nodes as a lease-like mechanism for failure detection and leader election recipes. Discuss lease renewal protocols and fencing tokens (fencing to prevent split-brain when a lease holder is wrongly presumed dead).

2) MEMBERSHIP CHANGES: Cover Raft's joint consensus (overlapping old/new configuration majorities) vs. single-server membership changes, the dangers of naive two-config-switch without joint consensus (disjoint majorities / double majority split-brain). Cover Paxos-style reconfiguration via special "reconfiguration" commands in the replicated log (state-machine-based reconfiguration, as in "Paxos Made Live" or "Vertical Paxos"). Cover primary-backup / ZooKeeper's dynamic reconfiguration (ZOOKEEPER-107, using a reconfig API with similar overlapping-majority safety). Cover SWIM protocol for scalable membership/failure detection in gossip-based systems (random probing, infection-style gossip dissemination, suspicion mechanism to reduce false positives).

Be exhaustive and precise, using correct terminology. Write in plain prose paragraphs aimed at a technically rigorous reader. Target roughly 700-900 words.

arguments.objective: Write a rigorous, in-depth technical section covering consistency models, distributed system failure modes, and foundational impossibility results.
arguments.instructions:
Produce a detailed technical writeup covering three areas with precise standard terminology:

1) CONSISTENCY MODELS: Cover linearizability (real-time total order, single-copy semantics), sequential consistency (program-order-respecting total order without real-time constraint), causal consistency (happens-before partial order preservation, including session guarantees like monotonic reads/writes, read-your-writes, writes-follow-reads), and eventual consistency (convergence given no new updates, including strong eventual consistency / CRDTs as a refinement). Mention the CAP theorem precisely (consistency/availability/partition-tolerance, Gilbert-Lynch formalization) and PACELC as its extension (latency/consistency tradeoff in the absence of partitions).

2) FAILURE MODES: Cover crash-stop/fail-stop failures, crash-recovery failures, omission failures (send/receive omission), timing failures (performance failures in synchronous systems), and Byzantine failures (arbitrary/malicious behavior) per the Byzantine Generals Problem. Discuss network partitions, asymmetric/partial partitions, and message loss/duplication/reordering assumptions in different system models (synchronous, asynchronous, partially synchronous per Dwork-Lynch-Stockmeyer).

3) IMPOSSIBILITY RESULTS: Cover FLP impossibility (Fischer-Lynch-Paterson, 1985 - no deterministic consensus algorithm can guarantee termination in an asynchronous system with even one crash failure), the CAP theorem's impossibility framing (Gilbert-Lynch 2002 proof), the Two Generals Problem as an illustrative unsolvable coordination problem under unreliable communication, and the implications for practical systems (why Raft/Paxos use randomized timeouts or rely on partial synchrony / failure detectors, referencing Chandra-Toueg failure detector classes, e.g. Omega, to circumvent FLP).

Be exhaustive and precise. Write in plain prose paragraphs aimed at a technically rigorous reader. Target roughly 700-900 words.
